Topic: Roman soldiers and the myth that they were paid in salt, Roman Empire, 1st century AD.
Constraint: about 110 words, short sentences.
Constraint: first sentence must be exactly: "You've heard Roman soldiers were paid in salt. They weren't."
Constraint: facts in order: (1) the word "salary" comes from Latin salarium, which in Roman texts simply means a money allowance (2) Pliny the Elder linked salt to the word, but no ancient source says soldiers were paid in salt (3) the "salt money" story was invented by 18th-century dictionary writers guessing at the word's origin (4, strongest) Roman soldiers were paid in coins, and the army deducted money for their food, clothes and weapons.
Constraint: frame the salt payment as a myth throughout; say "no ancient source" rather than "never".
Constraint: end on fact 4. No moral, no question, no call to action.
evaluationCases.scriptText: You've heard Roman soldiers were paid in salt. They weren't. In the Roman army, around the 1st century AD, soldiers earned a salarium. In Latin texts, that word simply meant a money allowance. Pliny the Elder once linked it to salt, but no ancient source says soldiers were paid in salt. The salt-payment story was actually invented later. Eighteenth-century dictionary writers guessed at the word's origin and ran with salt. It made a neat tale, but it's a myth. The truth is plainer. Roman soldiers were paid in coins, minted denarii. From that pay, the army deducted money for food, clothing, and weapons.

Topic: English farm workers and craftsmen after the Black Death, medieval England, 1351.
Constraint: about 150 words, short sentences.
Constraint: first sentence must be exactly: "In 1351, England made it a crime for workers to take a pay rise."
Constraint: facts in order: (1) the Black Death of 1348 to 1350 killed a huge share of England's people; historians' estimates mostly range from 40 to 60 percent (2) with so few workers left, the survivors demanded higher pay (3) the Statute of Labourers fixed daily pay at the old pre-plague rates: a master carpenter 3 pence, a master mason 4 pence, their helpers a penny and a half, hay-makers one penny (4) a worker who broke the law could be put in the stocks for three days or more, or sent to gaol (5, strongest) the law largely failed: farm wages in England roughly doubled between 1350 and 1450.
Constraint: use the helper's penny and a half as one day's work, worth $120 today. A master mason's legal day was worth nearly three helper days, about $320 today. Use "about".
Constraint: say "estimates range" for the death toll and "could be" for the punishments.
Constraint: end on fact 5. No moral, no question, no call to action.
evaluationCases.scriptText: In 1351, England made it a crime for workers to take a pay rise. The Black Death had just swept through, 1348 to 1350. Estimates range from forty to sixty percent of England's people dead. Survivors who lived saw their labor suddenly scarce. They demanded higher wages. Parliament answered with the Statute of Labourers, freezing pay at old rates. A master carpenter: three pence a day. A master mason: four pence. Helpers: a penny and a half. Hay-makers: one penny. That helper's wage, a penny and a half, was worth about one hundred twenty dollars today. The mason's legal maximum was worth about three hundred twenty. Breaking the law could mean the stocks for three days or more, or gaol. None of it worked. Between 1350 and 1450, farm wages roughly doubled anyway.

evaluationCases.scriptText: In 301 AD, a Roman emperor made overcharging for eggs a crime punishable by death. Prices were soaring across the empire, and Diocletian blamed greedy sellers for the panic. So he set official maximum prices for over a thousand goods, carved in stone for every market to see. Four eggs cost four denarii — about one sixth of a laborer's daily pay. But the law did not calm the chaos. A writer of the time claimed sellers hid their goods rather than sell at a loss, and prices only worsened. Blood was shed over bread and wine. So by 305 AD, when Diocletian stepped down, the law had largely failed, quietly ignored in markets everywhere. An emperor who could order executions could not control the price of an egg.

evaluationCases.scriptText: In 1850s London, children waded into the Thames mud for about three pennies a day. At low tide they searched for coal, iron, rope, bones, and copper nails torn loose from ships. It was filthy work, but it kept hungry families fed. So when journalist Henry Mayhew came looking for stories, he found these children along the riverbank and wrote them into his book, London Labour and the London Poor. But the numbers he recorded were bleak. Mayhew estimated a mudlark earned about three pence a day, while he put a dock labourer's wage at two shillings sixpence, about thirty pence. So the arithmetic was brutal. A whole day in the Thames mud was worth a tenth of a day on the docks above it.

A 2-minute explainer: how the Eiffel Tower was built, and why it was not torn down.
Use only these facts:
- The tower was built for the 1889 World's Fair in Paris, which marked 100 years since the French Revolution.
- It was designed at the engineering company of Gustave Eiffel; the first sketch came from Maurice Koechlin and Emile Nouguier.
- Construction took 2 years, 2 months and 5 days, from 1887 to 1889, and the tower opened on 31 March 1889.
- It is made of 18,038 pieces of wrought iron held together by 2.5 million rivets.
- At 300 metres it was the tallest man-made structure in the world until the Chrysler Building passed it in 1930.
- Its permit was for 20 years, after which the city could have dismantled it.
- Eiffel saved it by turning it into a scientific tool: he used it for meteorological and aerodynamic experiments and a radio antenna, so the city kept it.
Chapters should follow: why build it, how it went up, why it was almost lost, why it stayed.
evaluationCases.scriptText:
What almost happened to the most famous tower in the world? It was nearly torn down and sold for scrap, just twenty years after it opened. But before that, why was it built at all? The city needed a centerpiece for the 1889 World's Fair, marking one hundred years since the French Revolution. Designed at Gustave Eiffel's engineering company, the first sketch actually came from two of his engineers, Maurice Koechlin and Emile Nouguier, before Eiffel took the project forward.

How do you even build something that tall? Construction took two years, two months and five days, running from 1887 to 1889, and the tower opened on 31 March 1889. It was assembled from 18,038 pieces of wrought iron, held together by two and a half million rivets. At 300 metres, it became the tallest man-made structure on Earth, a title it would hold until the Chrysler Building overtook it in 1930.

So why was this record-breaking tower almost destroyed? Its construction permit was only for 20 years. Once that permit expired, the city of Paris had the right to dismantle it completely and clear the site. For a structure built purely as a temporary fairground centerpiece, that looked like the end.

So how did it survive? Eiffel turned his tower into a scientific tool the city couldn't afford to lose. He used it for meteorological and aerodynamic experiments, and later as a radio antenna, giving it a practical purpose beyond spectacle. That usefulness convinced the city to keep it standing instead of tearing it down. Next time you see it, remember it wasn't saved by beauty alone, but by the research still happening inside it.

evaluationCases.scriptText:
Today, many people worry that AI will take their job. People have worried about machines before, and history kept the receipts.

How did workers wake up before an alarm clock ended the knocker-upper's job? A knocker-upper woke workers with a long stick. That was the job: waking workers. But Mary Smith used a different tool in London's East End. She used a pea shooter and dried peas. So the story of the knocker-upper includes both the long stick and Mary Smith's pea shooter. The tools differed, but the task was waking workers. Mary Smith did that work from the 1900s to the 1930s, for sixpence a week. Those are the terms of this story: a worker who woke other workers, a pea shooter, dried peas, and sixpence a week. But cheap alarm clocks ended the job. So the job's ending belongs to the alarm clock, rather than to an account of what Mary Smith did next. She retired in 1934. The brief gives us her retirement, and it gives us the machine that ended the job. It does not give us her life after that. What we can follow is the task itself. Workers needed waking, and knocker-uppers did the waking. But cheap alarm clocks took over that task, so the job ended. Mary Smith's story gives that change a name, a place and a tool: Mary Smith in London's East End, with a pea shooter and dried peas.

Why did automatic elevators take more than 50 years to feel normal? Automatic elevators were invented around 1900. But they were not trusted. So invention was not the same thing as acceptance. An automatic elevator existed, but people did not trust it. In 1945, a New York strike stranded about 1.5 million office workers. That is the size of the disruption in this account. Owners pushed automatic elevators. So the automatic machine became the alternative that owners pushed. A calm recorded voice, a red stop button and an emergency phone are the details of that change. They belong together in this story: the voice, the button, the phone. But the change did not feel normal immediately. It took more than 50 years to feel normal. So a story that begins with an invention around 1900 cannot end at the invention. It has to include the lack of trust, the strike in 1945 and the owners pushing the automatic alternative. Today there are only a handful of operators. The operator's job did not remain as it had been, but the machine did not feel normal just because it had been invented. So the contrast is between having an automatic elevator and accepting an automatic elevator. The machine was automatic, but trust did not arrive with its invention. So the story includes the recorded voice, the stop button and the emergency phone, as well as the strike and the owners pushing automatic elevators. The invention came around 1900; feeling normal took more than 50 years. The strike stranded about 1.5 million office workers, and owners pushed the automatic elevators.

What did Dorothy Vaughan do when electronic computers arrived? She had joined NACA as a human computer in 1943. In 1949 she became acting head of West Area Computers, the first Black supervisor at NACA. That was her work before the electronic computers arrived. But electronic computers arrived in 1961. So the story turns from her position among human computers to what she did with the new computing work. She taught herself FORTRAN. She also taught her co-workers. Those are the actions in this account: learning FORTRAN herself and teaching her co-workers. But this is not a reason to invent a different ending for her. She retired in 1971. So the sequence stays with the facts: joining in 1943, acting head in 1949, electronic computers arriving in 1961, learning and teaching FORTRAN, retirement in 1971. Her story includes a machine arriving, but it also includes a worker learning. The human computer and the electronic computer belong to different parts of the account. Dorothy Vaughan belongs in both parts through the actions the brief records. She joined NACA, became acting head of West Area Computers and taught herself FORTRAN. So her co-workers belong in the story too: she taught them. We can tell that through scenes and silhouettes, without a portrait. The change in computing is part of the story, but learning and teaching are part of it too. Her retirement in 1971 closes the account given here.

Why did the cash machine not immediately end the bank teller? ATMs rolled out from the 1970s, with over 400,000 in the United States. But teller jobs did not fall as ATMs rolled out. So counting machines alone does not tell this story. Branch tellers fell from 20 to 13 between 1988 and 2004, but city branches rose 43 percent. There were fewer tellers per branch, but more city branches. So the change within a branch is not the same measure as the number of teller jobs. The teller's job became helping customers. That is the change in the work recorded here. But the account does not stop at the ATM rollout. Numbers fell later, in the smartphone era. So there are different changes to keep separate: fewer tellers in a branch, more city branches, a job becoming helping customers, and numbers falling later. The dates and figures belong to those changes. The 20 to 13 figure belongs to branch tellers between 1988 and 2004. The 43 percent figure belongs to the rise in city branches. The over 400,000 figure belongs to ATMs in the United States. But teller jobs did not fall as ATMs rolled out. So the later fall belongs to the smartphone era in this account. It is an ending that differs from the alarm clock ending the knocker-upper's job. It also differs from the long acceptance of automatic elevators and from Dorothy Vaughan learning FORTRAN. These accounts follow the workers as well as the machines, without predicting what AI will do. The cash machine didn't end the bank teller. The phone in your pocket did.

evaluationCases.scriptText:
In 2003, Lego was losing money fast.

How much money was missing? In 2003, the shortfall was about 1.4 billion Danish kroner, roughly 220 million dollars. Those are the figures at the start of this story. Then came 2004. Almost a thousand workers were laid off. The owner put about 800 million kroner of his own money into the company. That is where the story began.

So what did going back to basics mean? Instead of chasing growth, Lego went back to basics. In 2005, it sold its four Legoland theme parks for 375 million euros. The purpose was to focus on its core toys, going back to basics instead of chasing growth. The change was a return to the toys: the core business, with the brick at its center. This was the change at the center of the story: a return to the toys themselves. Think of the brick as the thread connecting the beginning and the end. The parks were sold, and the focus was the core toys.

Where did that leave Lego ten years later? In the first half of 2015, Lego outsold Mattel: 2.1 billion dollars against 1.9 billion. By sales, it was the world's biggest toy company. By sales matters here: that is the comparison these figures support. From the shortfall in 2003 to that sales comparison in 2015, the story turns back to the core toys. Lego won by going back to the brick.
